statements.quote: The course has covered what AI *is* and what it *can do*; this chapter is the part that decides what it *can afford to do* — and it is missing until now.

Economics is not a business afterthought bolted onto the technology; it is a **physical layer**, and it explains decisions you have already seen without a word of arithmetic: why the frontier moved to [Mixture of Experts](mixture_of_experts.php) (more knowledge, same active cost), why the field moved from large under-trained models toward smaller models trained on far more data ([Scaling](hyperparameters.php), \cite[Hoffmann et al., 2022]{hoffmann2022chinchilla}), and why "just run it locally" is sometimes the cheapest option and sometimes the most expensive.
The whole layer reduces to two numbers — *FLOPs for training* and *FLOPs per token for inference* — and everything below is arithmetic on top of those two.
Here is the load-bearing estimate.

statements.quote: The single most important serving cost-saver is **prompt caching**, and its arithmetic is the [prefill/decode split](inference_vs_training.php) you already met.
statements.section: Why caching saves ~10×: the prefill is paid once

statements.quote: The expensive part of a call is often the **prefill** — reading a long, *repeated* system prompt, tool definitions, or few-shot examples into context.
statements.section: Why caching saves ~10×: the prefill is paid once

statements.quote: Without caching, you pay the prefill FLOPs *every call*.
statements.section: Why caching saves ~10×: the prefill is paid once

statements.quote: With caching, the repeated prefix's keys and values are computed **once** and *reused*, so the second and later calls skip that prefill almost entirely.
statements.section: Why caching saves ~10×: the prefill is paid once

statements.quote: That is where the "~10×" comes from: when a call is dominated by a long, repeated prefix (say 4,000 tokens of system prompt) plus a short completion (say 400), uncached you pay for all 4,400 tokens' prefill+decode, but cached you pay mostly for the 400-token completion — roughly **one tenth** of the work per call.
statements.section: Why caching saves ~10×: the prefill is paid once

statements.quote: \cite[Anthropic, Prompt caching]{promptcaching} is the production example: cached tokens are billed at a fraction of uncached ones, precisely because the prefill that would have been recomputed is not.
statements.section: Why caching saves ~10×: the prefill is paid once

statements.quote: The calculator above models this directly — slide the cached fraction and watch the bill fall by up to ~90% on the cached part.
statements.section: Why caching saves ~10×: the prefill is paid once

statements.quote: The deeper point: caching is not a trick, it is a consequence of the two regimes.
statements.section: Why caching saves ~10×: the prefill is paid once

statements.quote: **Prefill is compute-bound and pay-once-able; decode is memory-bound and per-step.** Anything you can make *pay-once* (a repeated prefix) you should cache, because you are moving cost out of the per-call path and into a one-time one.
statements.section: Why caching saves ~10×: the prefill is paid once

statements.quote: The last comparison is the one people get wrong.
statements.section: 7B on a laptop, or the API: fixed cost vs per-token cost

statements.quote: "Run it locally" and "call the API" are not the same cost shape:
statements.section: 7B on a laptop, or the API: fixed cost vs per-token cost

statements.quote: * **The API is *per-token*.** You pay for what you use — zero when idle, high when busy.
statements.section: 7B on a laptop, or the API: fixed cost vs per-token cost

statements.quote: The marginal cost of a token is the price; there is no fixed cost.
statements.section: 7B on a laptop, or the API: fixed cost vs per-token cost

statements.quote: This is cheap for a **light, spiky** workload and expensive for a heavy, steady one (you keep paying per token forever).
statements.section: 7B on a laptop, or the API: fixed cost vs per-token cost

statements.quote: * **Local is *fixed*.** You pay for the hardware (a GPU that holds a 7B model) once, and then tokens cost almost nothing in compute — the marginal cost is just electricity.
statements.section: 7B on a laptop, or the API: fixed cost vs per-token cost

statements.quote: This is expensive for a **light** workload (you bought a GPU to use 2% of the time) and cheap for a **heavy, steady** one (the fixed cost amortizes to nothing over millions of tokens).
statements.section: 7B on a laptop, or the API: fixed cost vs per-token cost

statements.quote: They cross at a **breakeven**: local is better when your *steady* token volume is high enough that the hardware cost is recovered within your horizon; the API is better when your volume is light, spiky, or private-data-light.
statements.section: 7B on a laptop, or the API: fixed cost vs per-token cost

statements.quote: And there is a third axis the arithmetic ignores — **privacy**: local keeps the data on the machine, which is sometimes worth the worse economics.
statements.section: 7B on a laptop, or the API: fixed cost vs per-token cost

statements.quote: Caching moves the pay-once prefill out of the per-call path; the active-vs-total gap is what sparsity buys; and fixed-versus-per-token is what "local or API" really means.
statements.section: 7B on a laptop, or the API: fixed cost vs per-token cost

statements.quote: None of it is about the technology being *worth* it — it is about the technology being *affordable*, which is a different question, and the one that decides what gets built.
